Essentially, it guarantees that all system members receive the same information, even if certain malicious members deceive others by sending conflicting data. Existing broadcast protocols rely on a central point of trust, with specific groups (quorums) assumed to function reliably. This study focuses on a decentralized model where every participant establishes its own trusted groups (quorums). We introduce a set of relaxed broadcast abstractions tailored to these settings and develop an optimal broadcast protocol, which achieves the highest level of consistency by ensuring system members only receive the same information from a single source. Furthermore, we demonstrate the relationship between this optimal consistency and the parameters of a graph representing decentralized trust assumptions. We examine various possible network topologies in which broadcast can operate and find that a specific dual-fanout structure provides the balance between achieving the best consistency and minimizing the number of trusted groups required. We show that no broadcast protocol can achieve better consistency than this dual-fanout model. Finally, we highlight the practical implications of these results in a decentralized P2P setting. We modify an existing P2P algorithm to use a dual-fanout structure and find that it performs efficiently in random networks. Compared to alternatives that do not use a dual-fanout structure, this modified algorithm achieves better consistency with similar overhead. This work addresses a critical gap in reliable broadcast by considering diverse decentralized trust models, providing fundamental insights into broadcast consistency, and delivering better performance than previous approaches. This paper presents a proof of two significant results for relatively free Lie algebras with specific properties: a generalized version of Shirshov's theorem and an extension of Kharlampovich's Freiheitssatz theorem. These findings are built upon previous work by Kharlampovich and Weilganter, and involve exploiting the properties of reduced words within relatively free Lie algebras. A key step in the proof involves establishing a conclusion based on the concept of'special' subalgebras, which themselves can be broken down into simpler components using the properties of reduced words. This line of reasoning ultimately leads to two important consequences: the first confirms Shirshov's theorem for Lie algebras generated by two elements, while the second asserts the Freiheitssatz theorem for any relatively free Lie algebra defined over a specific set of non-commutative variables. Notably, this second result significantly expands upon the original scope of Freiheitssatz theorem as initially proven by Kharlampovich and Weilganter, and sets a new standard for Lie algebras. Additionally, the paper takes a critical approach in defining what constitutes'special' subalgebras, which themselves give rise to interesting one-parameter groups within relatively free Lie algebras. This novel formulation not only provides a more streamlined and unified understanding of existing one-parameter groups but also opens up new avenues for further exploration and generalization. One notable phenomenon is that noise can induce entirely new states in a system that wouldn't exist in its noise-free state. Researchers have studied this phenomenon in complex systems like insect colonies and fish, observing how noise can cause collective behaviors to emerge. In a new study, researchers investigated whether this phenomenon occurs in quantum systems as well, and found evidence of a new classically forbidden transition induced by quantum noise. They used a simple mathematical model of a system that can be studied analytically to explore how noise causes it to switch into a stable limit cycle state. What they found is that the noise-induced transition in the quantum system has properties that are fundamentally different from those found in classical systems, and that are also unique to quantum systems. These findings reveal a significant distinction between how noise behaves in quantum versus classical systems. The research highlights a potential limitation of using classical models to study quantum systems, and may have implications for how we design experiments to study noise-induced phenomena in quantum systems. The specific system studied is special because it has a balance point that is stable in the absence of limit cycle behavior, but becomes unstable when the system enters a limit cycle state. This type of system is relatively rare in physics, but the research shows that noise can induce a new out-of-equilibrium dynamics in this system, and reveals complex dynamics that are not yet fully understood. The possibility of tuning quantum systems to replicate this phenomenon experimentally is also considered.

CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to recognize patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-based approach for identifying and outlining esophageal tumors.

To accomplish this, our study enhances the field of view for deep neural networks using two core components from the visual processing systems of vertebrates, known as on-center and off-center pathways. This pathway system consists of excitatory centers and inhibitory surrounds, and we refer to it as OOCS for simplicity. The on-center pathway responds positively to the presence of light within its core area but not in its periphery, while the off-center pathway responds positively to the absence of light within its core area but not in its periphery. Our OOCS pathways are developed using a difference of Gaussians, with the variance calculated analytically based on the size of the receptive fields. This pathway system effectively complements each other's responses to light stimuli, enabling a robust edge-detection ability, and ultimately leads to more accurate and reliable inferences in challenging lighting environments. This advantage is further quantified by evaluating the networks on the MVIT dataset, which contains video recordings from a microvehicle navigating through diverse lighting conditions. Our analysis reveals that the OOCS edge representation enhances the general illumination-resistance of deep neural networks by allowing the network to adapt to the dynamic lighting conditions over the course of the video sequence. Model uncertainty, also referred to as epistemic uncertainty, is a concept that measures a model's expected prediction error beyond random noise. In this paper, a novel metric called pathwise epistemic uncertainty for estimating Q-value functions is introduced, accompanied by a method for approximating its upper limit known as the F-value. In particular, the enhancements resulted in a 5.5% increase in average rewards for the HalfCheetah-v2 task and a 2.5% increase in average rewards for the Walker2d-v2 task. Wiman's work presents an argument that a degree-nine polynomial can be solved using one four-variable algebraic function, along with additional irrationalities up to degree five. Notably, his reasoning hinges on a particular assumption regarding generic intersections in affine space, which lacks formal proof. Nonetheless, his findings significantly influence the understanding of rational points on quintic varieties, particularly in the case of Schur's conjecture, which was later confirmed by Kleiman and Zariski through independent works. This translated paper maintains the original notation and formatting as the original publication. 

In this updated version, I've included an additional section (located after the reference list), which presents modern approaches to validating Wiman's interesection hypothesis, thus providing a more comprehensive validation of his initial claims. 

It's worth noting that Wiman's work also touches on the specific case of degree-nine polynomials in affine 4-space, which was independently explored by Blower in a more recent publication from 2019. 

I hope this translated paper, along with the included supplementary material, can serve as a useful resource for those interested in algebraic geometry and the study of rational points on varieties.

To create more robust world representations, AI architecture can be modified to process and learn from different input types, yet current multi-sensory AI only yields slight improvements over those trained with single-sensory input.

To bridge this knowledge gap, Germany's Industry 4.0 initiative introduced the Administrative Shell concept to facilitate the representation of digitized information about physical systems and software platforms.  In this paper, a digital representation model based on RDF and OWL is proposed, addressing the complexities of Industry 4.0 through semantic technologies.  We demonstrate our approach, referred to as the Semantic I4.0 Component, by showcasing a real-world use case exemplifying its effectiveness in streamlining Industry 4.0 communications and comprehension.  By promoting the use of established standards, such as RDF and OWL, we aim to foster a unified, shared understanding of digitized information to support seamless interactions between systems and promote more effective decision-making.  Our work represents a significant step towards harnessing the potential of semantic technologies to drive Industry 4.0 evolution and implementation.  We hope that by addressing these challenges through our model, a more cohesive and unified digitized information landscape can be created, ultimately benefiting Industry 4.0 stakeholders.  By openly sharing our approach, we intend to encourage and facilitate the adoption of digitized information within Industry 4.0 settings. Additionally, we established sufficient conditions for stochastic ultimate boundedness, stochastic permanence, mean persistence, mean weak persistence, and the extinction of solutions in this model. Our study also provides a specific example to illustrate our findings, and the results obtained in this paper can be extended to a broader class of autonomous systems. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the stochastic ultimate boundedness implies both stochastic permanence and mean persistence. In contrast, mean weak persistence does not necessarily ensure stochastic ultimate boundedness. Moreover, the condition for the model to go to extinction is opposite to the condition for stochastic ultimate boundedness, mean permanence, and mean persistence. Ultimately, the condition for ultimate boundedness is stronger than the condition for permanent coexistence and persistence. This study contributes to our understanding of non-autonomous stochastic predator-prey model behaviors and highlights the importance of considering random factors in ecological models, especially when the population is on the verge of extinction. In real-world applications, this knowledge can aid in making informed decisions to prevent population decline or extinction. In contrast, failing to account for random factors may lead to inaccurate conclusions about model behavior. For instance, it is not necessarily true that reducing the intensity of the noise will guarantee the long-term survival of a species; in fact, a lower noise intensity may increase the risk of population decline or extinction.

Typically, strict conditions need to be met to achieve synchronization, but research has revealed that slight discrepancies in parameters or connections do not necessarily preclude it. Finally, it is suggested that experiments could be designed to induce group synchronization in disparate systems, offering avenues for future research and exploration. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Secondly, they combine pseudo-labels with actual labels using the same loss function, failing to acknowledge their distinct contributions to classification. To address these limitations, we propose InfoGNN, an innovative pseudo-labeling framework. InfoGNN focuses on labeling nodes with the greatest informative value, which effectively represents local neighborhoods through mutual information maximization. To counterbalance the risks of pseudo-label noise and class imbalance, we also incorporate a modified cross-entropy loss with class-balanced regularization in the model re-training process. Comprehensive experiments on six graph datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, which outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and robust self-supervised methods on graph-related tasks. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Boundary Estimation Network (DBEN), which circumvents the drawbacks of traditional boundary estimation methods. DBEN views action boundaries within a video as semantically discrete points and directly estimates the boundaries in an implicit latent space. Unlike existing methods that generate proposals with continuous or nearby semantics, DBEN achieves distinct proposal generation by introducing a regularization term in the loss function. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean feature vectors for every encountered class. This basic approach achieved 88.53% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art continual learning methods and highlighting the robustness of pre-trained models in addressing the problem of continual learning. In a broader context, this study contributes to the growing theme of exploring robust and understandable machine learning systems.

This paper presents a proof of two significant results for relatively free Lie algebras with specific properties: a generalized version of Shirshov's theorem and an extension of Kharlampovich's Freiheitssatz theorem. These findings are built upon previous work by Kharlampovich and Weilganter, and involve exploiting the properties of reduced words within relatively free Lie algebras. A key step in the proof involves establishing a conclusion based on the concept of'special' subalgebras, which themselves can be broken down into simpler components using the properties of reduced words. This line of reasoning ultimately leads to two important consequences: the first confirms Shirshov's theorem for Lie algebras generated by two elements, while the second asserts the Freiheitssatz theorem for any relatively free Lie algebra defined over a specific set of non-commutative variables. Notably, this second result significantly expands upon the original scope of Freiheitssatz theorem as initially proven by Kharlampovich and Weilganter, and sets a new standard for Lie algebras. Additionally, the paper takes a critical approach in defining what constitutes'special' subalgebras, which themselves give rise to interesting one-parameter groups within relatively free Lie algebras. This novel formulation not only provides a more streamlined and unified understanding of existing one-parameter groups but also opens up new avenues for further exploration and generalization. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. To address this, a novel, well-established global pooling framework has been developed through the lens of optimal transport theory. By allowing the parameters of this problem to be learned, various global pooling methods are unified within a single framework. In this research, we tackle a critical challenge associated with slow training convergence in DETR and introduce a conditional cross-attention mechanism to accelerate DETR training. The motivation behind our approach stems from the reliance of DETR's cross-attention on high-quality content embeddings to accurately identify objects' extremities and predict their boundaries. Consequently, this increases the complexity of content embedding requirements and, in turn, the difficulty of training. To address this limitation, we have developed a method called conditional DETR, which trains a decoder embedding-dependent conditional spatial query. The effectiveness of our approach lies in enabling each cross-attention head to target specific object regions or parts within those regions. This enables cross-attention heads to effectively concentrate on a reduced spatial range for localizing distinctive areas relevant to object classification and box regression, thus minimizing dependence on content embeddings and making the training process easier. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our conditional DETR model exhibits significantly accelerated training speeds, particularly a 6.7 times faster convergence for backbone networks R50 and R101 and a 10 times faster convergence for the stronger backbones DC5-R50 and DC5-R101. The implementation of a single bit per attribute instead of floating-point values significantly reduces the size of data structures while maintaining or improving the quality. Our experiments using real data replicate a personalized search task, demonstrating a straightforward technique to combine the bit vectors leads to a substantial improvement in processing speed with minimal reduction in accuracy. Our findings show that using bit vectors for this specific task results in a 5 to 7 times faster operation than traditional methods. The observed speedup is largely due to reducing memory access costs. Although our experiments focused on a specific scenario, the underlying technique is versatile and can be adapted to a variety of other tasks, such as image processing and data mining. Our work also explores the limitations and potential risks of this method. It highlights the importance of evaluating both the effectiveness and efficiency of algorithms. In addition, our research identifies two areas where the combination of bit vectors with existing techniques may yield improved performance and provides avenues for future research in this domain. Our study can be used as a reference for evaluating the performance of algorithms in tasks that involve a large amount of data processing and require fast results, such

Although established methods like bisimulation minimization can take advantage of these patterns, they operate directly on the explicit state model, ignoring the program-level structure. In contrast, there has been little research on reducing structured state spaces by reasoning directly about the high-level program. This paper presents a new, fully automatic method to reduce Markov models based on the program's structure. The technique calculates the summarized behavior of adjacent locations in the program's flow diagram, resulting in a model with fewer global patterns. The experiment results show that this method is effective in practice, leading to significant reductions in state space size for a range of benchmark and industrial models. In comparison with other state reduction techniques, this method tends to perform better in terms of a metric for summarized behavior similarity. The method's underlying algorithm improves upon previous work by using a more efficient method to establish relations between structured state components. To mitigate this issue, gradual verification has been proposed, integrating static and dynamic checks to accommodate partial, complete, or absent specifications. Although it has been extended to cover recursive data structures on the heap, gradual verification has a significant drawback - users do not reap the benefit of decreased dynamic checks as specifications improve, and all properties continue to be dynamically verified regardless of any static guarantees. Moreover, a full-fledged gradual verifier does not exist, hindering the evaluation of its performance and applicability.

We developed Gradual C0, a practical gradual verifier for C0, a safe subset of C, specifically designed for educational purposes, to fill this gap. To optimize the insertion of dynamic checks and enhance efficiency, Gradual C0 focuses on attributing types to expression results rather than establishing a full-typeing system. This approach facilitates the effective elimination of unnecessary dynamic checks as specifications improve. Moreover, we introduced a novel concept known as verification density, which quantifies the extent to which a program's behavior is statically guaranteed. This allows us to assess the performance of Gradual C0 and demonstrate significant speedups for typical programs, averaging a 2.4 times faster verification time. Finally, we investigate the maximum achievable verification density for 17 benchmark programs and explore potential optimization opportunities for further improvement. This study aims to promote the development and evaluation of gradual verifiers. To facilitate this, we publicly release Gradual C0, allowing others to test and modify

Yet, the rapidly increasing complexity of scientific code coupled with the short lifespan of IT technologies poses significant obstacles to successfully recreating the data analysis environment, despite source code accessibility. There is a notable discrepancy between having version-controlled code and actually establishing an operational data analysis environment. We propose the creation of a snapshotting file system optimized for distributing software, which allows the preservation of varied data analysis environments. This is exemplified by our approach in replicating the data analysis software used to find the Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider. We demonstrate the feasibility of restoring a 2012 data analysis environment on a modern 2017 Linux-based system, despite changes in hardware and software during the intervening five-year period. This is accomplished by developing a custom file system, which incorporates multiple facets of knowledge: (a) the ability to retain consistency when transferring data analysis environments to different systems, (b) the ability to track dependencies on specific software distributions and versions, and (c) the ability to compensate for differences in hardware and software between the original and target systems. We successfully tested the file system, which allows a 2017 system to recreate a 2012 data analysis environment on various Linux-based systems. Additionally, we evaluated the performance implications of relying on this file system. This file system concept can facilitate the consistent implementation of software snapshots across diverse scientific disciplines. It can aid in the preservation of many data analysis environments,

The primary issue lies in current travel demand modeling methods, which often generate overly optimistic and unrealistic trips that fail to reflect actual passenger choices. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of "mini activities" - short tasks that travelers perform during their journeys - to explain the divergence between simulated and observed trips. By utilizing data from smart cards, we can uncover these mini activities and incorporate them into the simulated trips. By applying this approach, we can build a more accurate Markov chain for trip simulations, which effectively minimizes discrepancies between planned and observed trips. Experimental results obtained from testing on a dataset of passenger trips in Nancy, France, demonstrate substantial improvements in reducing these discrepancies. Additionally, our framework has the potential to provide actionable insights to transportation planners by uncovering underlying passenger behaviors and preferences. We found that a significant proportion of the detected mini activities correspond to actual passenger activities, with the remaining fraction potentially representing other forms of travel-related data, such as micro-activities. In particular, our analysis revealed that even in the simplest Standard Model extensions, such as single scalar singlets or neutral triplets, some positivity bounds can be violated. Our findings indicate that, if positivity bounds are breached in experimental data, it may not necessarily imply unitarity, causality breakdown, or new light degrees of freedom. However, when considering probabilities, this challenge is even more complicated: research has demonstrated that under the constraint of differential privacy, there are data sources for which the best-case EO comes at a cost of total accuracy loss - meaning an EO-compliant model can only match a simple classifier in terms of accuracy. Counterfactual inverse-propensity-scoring has been the traditional approach to unbiased click-based learning-to-rank. Notably, doubly-robust estimation methods have yet to be applied to click-based learning-to-rank tasks in prior literature. This paper presents a novel doubly-robust estimator tailored specifically for addressing position-bias issues in click data, which does not provide direct observability of the treatment - user examination. To resolve this challenge, the estimator employs the expected treatment per rank instead of the actual treatment, a characteristic that sets it apart from existing doubly-robust methods. This novel estimator surpasses the existing inverse-propensity-scoring approach in robustness, and significantly reduces variance in its estimates: experimental results reveal a dramatic reduction in required datapoints for optimal performance. Overall, the doubly-robust estimator makes notable contributions to the unbiased learning-to-rank field by achieving enhanced state-of-the-art performance and providing the most robust theoretical guarantees compared to existing estimators. Finally, a unified theoretical framework for deriving variance bounds for doubly-robust estimators in biased tasks is established, which is a previously unsolved problem in the literature. the development of Private Inference (PI). PI's unique attribute lies in concealing both the client's sensitive information and the trained model utilized by the service provider. Present-day PI methods rely on advanced encryption techniques like Homomorphic Encryption (HE), Secret Sharing (SS), Garbled Circuits (GC), and Oblivious Transfer (OT) to maintain confidentiality, however, these methods inevitably reveal computational evidence of both the client and server. This paper breaks new ground in PI by dispensing with the need for specific cryptographic evidence, while still upholding confidentiality. Our core contribution is the Integrated Homomorphic Encryption (IHE), a novel protocol that fuses the advantages of HE, SS, and GC, allowing for the execution of both arithmetic operations and conditional statements in an encrypted manner. This concept is applied to Private Inference, as we present a unified framework that combines previous PI methods, while also introducing two novel approaches, both of which demonstrate improved efficiency compared to the current state-of-the-art. Our findings are substantiated by practical testing on real-world datasets, conducted using the OpenTIMIT speech recognition benchmark, where we successfully eliminated exposure to the trained model and client data, achieving a significant reduction in computation and network overhead compared to the best available alternative. The proposed models and code are publicly available for review and evaluation. This research is affiliated with the University of Edinburgh and conducted under the EPSRC DAppER grant (EP/S50150X/1). ```

This requirement is most pronounced in the analysis of high-resolution phase-contrast images of materials. Although commonly used electron scattering simulations based on atomic structures provide quick results with decent accuracy for many cases, particularly in scanning transmission electron microscopy, this simplification omits a critical aspect of electron scattering influenced by the material's molecular bonds. However, the advent of more sophisticated instruments and techniques allows for extracting a vast amount of data from electron microscopy, making it essential to utilize techniques that provide more detailed information such as 4D-STEM and ptychography to gain a deeper insight into materials' atomic structure. Therefore, to accurately analyze these increasingly detailed images, users are shifting towards more advanced simulation tools like wave-based scattering simulations that incorporate the material's molecular bonds. This paper reviews the progress in the field of electron scattering simulations with a focus on their practical applications and the potential of these advanced simulations to provide more precise insights into materials' atomic structure. Considering the rapidly increasing availability of powerful computational resources, integrating machine learning algorithms into these advanced simulations can significantly enhance their efficiency and make them more accessible to a broader range of users. This integration can significantly accelerate the analysis of large datasets collected from 4D-STEM and ptychography experiments. Moreover, the paper discusses the prospects of employing these advanced simulations in conjunction with machine learning to automate the interpretation of electron microscopy images and diffraction patterns. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. , finding precise solutions to combinatorial optimization problems can be extremely challenging, often becoming computationally infeasible as problem sizes increase. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and enabled public verification of trade requests by introducing a new verifiable double-sided auction type, which combines features of open and sealed auctions.

The verifiable double-sided auction offers a choice between two mechanisms: a proportional price matching mechanism and a worst-order matching mechanism. The former guarantees that a buyer receives at least the intended amount of currency and a seller receives at least the intended amount of currency, while the latter ensures that a buyer pays at most a specific price and a seller receives at least the intended amount of currency.

To achieve this verifiable double-sided auction type, we used advanced homomorphic encryption and fully homomorphic encryption techniques, which allowed us to perform private computation of the auction outcome. The main challenge we faced was finding an efficient way to calculate the worst-order matching mechanism in a privacy-preserving setting. To overcome this limitation, we developed a new protocol, which combined existing solutions to achieve a private auction calculation, while reducing the overall communication and computation complexity.

Our work evaluated the proposed verifiable double-sided auction type through experiments, which demonstrated its practicality in real-world applications, even when dealing with large quantities of trade requests. The experiments involved comparing the performance of the proportional price matching mechanism and the worst-order matching mechanism, which showed that the latter offered more robust protection against unfair behaviors.

focused on signal sampling, we investigated the computational efficiency of a method known as sparse sensing, derived from co-prime sensing theory. To improve sampling efficiency and flexibility, we developed a generalized framework, Diophantine sensing, by combining Diophantine equation principles and a high-order sparse measurement technique. The proposed Diophantine framework brings two major benefits: Firstly, it allows for more efficient frequency estimation, as the number of required samples becomes linearly dependent on the number of degrees of freedom and snapshots used. Secondly, for direction-of-arrival estimation, we devised two universal methods for constructing sparse arrays with large sensor distances, including one that achieves almost optimal array designs with very large sensor distance ratios. We further demonstrated that the number of required samples becomes linearly dependent on the number of degrees of freedom and frequencies (or directions) of arrival, making the Diophantine framework more efficient in practice. A numerical study is presented to validate the computational performance of the proposed framework. The conventional co-prime sensing method is also compared to the Diophantine framework, showing that the latter consistently outperforms the former, especially in scenarios with limited sample support. We concluded that the Diophantine framework offers more efficient sparse sensing with better performance, making it more suitable for various signal processing tasks. The proposed framework has potential applications in numerous other high-order sparse measurement techniques, thereby contributing to the development of more efficient sparse sensing tools. These techniques are classified into two groups: those using artificial intelligence to extract features but traditional algorithms for security, and those using AI to generate secure templates directly. We examine the benefits and drawbacks of each method, as well as how they are evaluated in terms of accuracy, security, and the ability to prevent reuse. While accuracy is typically assessed using standard evaluation methods, security and link prevention are often estimated or discussed in general terms rather than being thoroughly tested. By considering this distorted potential within the framework of three-dimensional semiconductor systems with cylindrical confinement, it becomes evident that lattice deformation introduces significant quantitative distinctions. For example, the distorted potential decreases the effective cyclotron frequency, ultimately resulting in increased Hall conductivity. Moreover, numerical simulations reveal that resistance fluctuations in these systems follow a power law dependent on the electron density, rather than a Gaussian distribution as seen in clean systems. Lastly, the presence of cylindrical confinement is shown to increase the resistance compared to a flat sample under the same conditions. All these effects are anticipated to appear in materials with a small band gap, such as trigonal InSb and heterostructures based on HgTe, as well as other materials with cylindrical confinement. The findings presented here can also be extended to studying resistance fluctuations in 2D electron gases under the influence of quantum Hall fluids and other excited quantum states. The research offers a valuable tool for investigating the behavior of electron systems in cylindrical nanosystems. The study also provides a framework for comparing experimental data with theoretical predictions in both cylindrical and beaked quantum Hall systems. The interface between the beaked and cylindrical shapes can generate distinctive resistance fluctuations and Hall conductivity patterns that can be replicated in both types of systems. The cylindrical geometry can be used to reproduce these patterns by increasing the resistance while maintaining the same electron density.

requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, designed to improve performance in multi-goal scenarios by selectively retaining both short-term and long-term memories. 
The short-term memory in MemoNav stores dynamic agent topological maps, updated as navigation progresses. To augment this memory, a graph attention module aggregates past short-term memories to generate long-term memories.
A forgetting module using a Transformer decoder retains only the informative fraction of the short-term memory, ensuring that both the updated short-term memory and the accumulated long-term memory are integrated into the working memory, guiding action generation.
Experimental evaluations of MemoNav on a new dataset demonstrate significantly better performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches using a fraction of the navigation history, with reduced instances of deadlock situations.

We consider slow rotation as classical, unassociated with the influence of the magnetic field, with the rotational speed $\Omega$ much lower than $\sqrt{qB}$. Our findings reveal, using an exact Dirac equation solution, that the intensity and spectrum of radiation and its handedness can be determined. We provide further evidence of an energy increase of radiation intensity via explicit numerical calculations and how rotational effects vary significantly according to magnetic and charge orientations. Moreover, we show that rotational effects are quantitatively substantial when the ratio of rotational speed to the cyclotron frequency is greater than $10^{-5}$, unaffected by spin until this threshold is exceeded, at which point it significantly affects radiation intensity and handedness. Additionally, we identify certain conditions under which rotational effects are negligible for circular polarization but decidedly present for linear polarization, thereby enabling experimental verification. Finally, we demonstrate that rotational effects are an essential feature, influenced by both magnetic and charge, to be considered in any accurate theory of particles undergoing Penrose processes. It is noted that our numerical estimates are based on the assumption that the rotational speed of particles is less than $10^{16}$ rad/s, a condition generally expected to apply in external magnetic fields. However, in the absence of an external magnetic field, or when the rotational speed exceeds the cyclotron frequency, the conventional spin polarization concept must be redefined.

In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. To date, the most effective methods approach these tasks as sequence-to-sequence problems reliant on substantial parallel training data. However, this paper proposes an iterative editing strategy that omits the need for parallel data. By leveraging a pre-trained Transformer model with masked language modeling and attribute classification, the editing process unfolds in a two-stage sequence during inference. First, the text representation dynamically adjusts to suit an attribute-driven goal. Then, a text span is selectively masked, and a novel alternative is generated conditioned on the optimized representation. Empirical tests on two prominent text revision tasks – text formalization and text simplification – reveal the superiority of our method. - It presents an unsupervised text revision technique grounded in iterative editing.

Many scenarios, such as working with type-specific Abstract Syntax Trees, inherently involve both pattern matching and generic hierarchies, necessitating proper compiler support. Compilers can address this problem by incorporating subtyping reconstruction: the ability to revive subtyping information that arises during pattern matching runtime. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind sudden population changes in this ecosystem, a simulation of the full model is conducted, where temporary, small-scale movements in predator populations are engineered to test their effects. The results demonstrate that in many cases, these small-scale movements can trigger, and sometimes hinder, the occurrence of S-shaped curves, leading to changes in ecosystem dynamics. The implementation of early warning indicators for detecting such events is explored, where the study of this model reveals that variations in predator separation can signal a forthcoming sudden change in ecosystem dynamics. This research contributes to our understanding of detecting and analyzing critical transitions in complex systems, providing a framework for recognizing and intervening in unfolding tipping points in biology, ecology, and other related fields. Various foundational studies aim to develop a universal mathematical framework for the theory, starting by characterizing the inherent structure of state and effect spaces within individual systems and their interaction rules. Despite being versatile, such a general framework allows multiple consistent rules for combining multiple systems when individual subsystems exhibit quantum characteristics. However, for bipartite systems, these rules fall short in producing correlations that exceed quantum expectations, especially in space-like relationships. In contrast, our findings indicate that similar bipartite combinations can facilitate non-quantum correlations in time-like relationships, implying unique functions for state and effect cones. We discuss how these correlations influence communication tasks and propose a way to verify the composition of fundamental particles through practical experiments. The advancement of quantum technology up to 100 qubits is accelerating, and therefore developing more efficient methods to simulate quantum systems becomes increasingly crucial. Especially crucial is the ability to accurately predict ground state properties of quantum systems which is linked to energy levels, magnetic moments, and other important characteristics. The variational hybrid algorithm, particularly the VQE method, has become the most reliable method for simulating quantum systems and is widely used in experiments. The critical component of the VQE algorithm is the quantum circuit that combines variational parameters with a classical optimization technique to precisely estimate expectation values. The variational circuit typically comprises a layered structure of single-qubit rotations and entangling gates, and choosing the correct circuit is challenging due to the vast search space. The layered architecture of the circuit resembles a digital computer's processing unit, and applying standard routing algorithms could significantly reduce the computational costs. The application of traffic routing algorithms, specifically the shortest path routing, to the variational quantum circuit has shown promising results by determining the optimal placement of two-qubit gates that connect distant qubits. The approach has been tested on quantum simulations of helium and lithium hydride molecules, and the efficient placement of entangling gates has led to notable improvements in the simulation's computational performance. The method can potentially be used in near-term quantum devices

By applying matrix element techniques, production and decay mechanisms of Higgs boson are identified, and its sensitivity is enhanced. Our approach exploits the camera's motion to separate objects into two categories, utilizing a rigid body assumption to estimate motion. We test this method on a newly created dataset featuring vehicle backgrounds and find that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, with results showing that the self-supervised approach improves overall accuracy by 2.5% and reduces errors related to moving objects by 10% compared to standard training methods. Additionally, our framework successfully captures the camera's motion, enabling the use of motion data in future research to develop more advanced autonomous driving applications. Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. The goal of this research is to investigate the feasibility of using machine learning to define the treated area in LITT, which would provide valuable clinical information and facilitate surgical decision-making. A total of 110 LITT patients treated at our institution were selected for this study, with their pre- and post-LITT MRI scans evaluated by two neuroradiologists who identified the treated region manually. We used these manual annotations to train support vector machines, which were then used to define the treated region in an independent test set of 30 patients, with accurate results obtained. In particular, the extracted features 'ClinRad' offered the best performance, with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.90, along with high Dice scores of 0.79 ± 0.20. These results demonstrate that machine learning based on radiological features can accurately define the treated area in LITT, which may contribute to improved surgical outcomes for epilepsy patients. Future research will leverage deep learning to further improve these initial machine learning results, with the aim of providing a fully automated solution for LITT. A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.

This study aims to shed light on the source of this vulnerability by investigating the effect of suboptimal components in pre-trained Transformer encoders, focusing on the Query and Value layers of self-attention mechanisms. During pre-training, these layers compete to capture essential information, but their individual abilities are hindered by suboptimal layers, leading to a phenomenon of overspecialization. When only a small part of the components is pruned post-pretraining, the remaining layers can no longer effectively utilize the learned information, resulting in substantial performance decline. To address this issue, the authors introduced a novel method called Self-Attention Refactorization (SAR), allowing the pruning of up to 85% of the components with only a minimal performance loss, and demonstrated its superiority over current compression techniques, including channel pruning, knowledge distillation, and hardware-based approaches like Tensor-Parallelism, PipeParallel, and Pipewise. Thoroughly tested on 8 different models and 5 diverse datasets, SAR showcased its remarkable ability to efficiently compress pre-trained Transformer encoders while minimizing the resulting performance loss. Following the successful application of SAR to compress pre-trained Transformer encoders, the authors explored its potential to streamline the process of fine-tuning these models, eliminating the need for costly, time-consuming iterations of pre-training and fine-tuning.

The four pillars of Confident AI comprise Repeatability, Believability, Sufficiency, and Adaptability. Each pillar is utilized to investigate underlying challenges in existing AI/ML systems and collectively offer a comprehensive approach to constructing reliable AI models. Specifically, we use CAI to analyze the predictability of popular Deep Neural Networks, examining how the Repeatability aspect is affected by model architecture, dataset, and prediction evaluation methods. Our findings highlight that repeated predictions from trained Deep Neural Networks are consistent, but the corresponding confidence intervals often capture the true classification accuracy rate less than 50%. The results suggest that, from a Confident AI perspective, the reliability of model forecasts depends not only on the consistency of predictions but also on the accuracy of the confidence provided. Therefore, in addition to optimizing repeatable predictions, it is essential to optimize the breadth and coverage of prediction intervals. The Confident AI framework can be applied to a wide range of AI/ML systems to balance their reliability and user trust, ultimately contributing to the construction of trustworthy AI models. The experiment used sealed water phantoms, created through 3D printing, that were exposed to X-rays, protons, and carbon ions at varying intensities up to 340 Gy per second. Oxygen levels were measured using an optical sensor that enabled non-invasive detection. The results revealed that oxygen consumption is solely dependent on the radiation's dose, rate, and energy transfer. Oxygen levels decreased by 0.04-0.18 percent per 10 Gy for 225-kV X-rays, 0.04-0.25 percent per 10 Gy for 224 MeV protons, and 0.09-0.17 percent per 10 Gy for carbon ions. Oxygen consumption slowed as the radiation intensity increased, due to the self-interactions of radicals at higher dose rates, resulting in reduced oxygen consumption at these higher rates. The researchers also found that clinical doses did not completely deplete oxygen levels, even at 10 Gy dose delivery. Ultimately, the study concluded that Flash radiation does deplete oxygen but not to the point of total depletion, with higher dose rates actually resulting in lower oxygen consumption than standard radiotherapy rates. A variety of innovative methods have been developed in an attempt to surpass supervised alternatives. A major challenge in SSL lies in ensuring that its approaches remain robust across different environments. This paper marks a first in acknowledging that SSL has inherent limitations arising from its reliance on a single guiding principle. To overcome these limitations, we have leveraged uncertainty representation to create a more robust and universally applicable hierarchical training protocol that is compatible with any existing SSL model. This improved approach is based on a fundamental concept called the information bottleneck principle and decomposes the feature learning process into two distinct training phases with separate supervision mechanisms. This dual-supervision strategy encompasses two pivotal steps: 1) data augmentation invariance and 2) fuzzy pseudo-labeling that incorporates both hard and soft annotation techniques. This novel protocol allows for learning shared features across multiple classes and categories and achieves its goal through a combination of data augmentation invariance and pseudo-labeling of distorted samples. We have evaluated our protocol in both traditional and cross-domain scenarios, contrasting it with existing methods that focus on cross-domain adaptation and feature learning. Our findings demonstrate that it offers consistent and high-performance outcomes across various benchmarks. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by dynamically adjusting the training loss function to prioritize performance-based tracking. This novel approach enables agents to rapidly learn and attain high performance in previously unexplored environments. Experimental evaluations across multiple scenarios demonstrate that CoIL surpasses traditional imitation learning methods in scenarios where rapid learning is crucial, while maintaining comparable results in scenarios where exploration is slower. Furthermore, we uncover key factors influencing CoIL's success and propose enhancements to tackle potential pitfalls. This study makes significant contributions to the field of Co-Imitation Learning and offers valuable insights for future research. The precision of this discretization is determined by a finite parameter, p, which approaches infinity. As p approaches infinity, the standard discretization approach converges to a continuum, whereas this model converges to a singular quantum mechanic state. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the protocols they use. To test the quantum superiority of this model, we designed a simple verification process requiring only single-qubit preparation, which runs on the same model as the original sampler on a grid structure with only a slight increase in computational resources. We further modified this process twice to be more robust against potential errors while preserving non-interactive properties, resulting in the first scheme having a reduced computational overhead based on standard error correction techniques, and the second scheme having a greater overhead but a significantly higher error tolerance (1.97%). Both modified verification processes are thought to be resistant to classical simulations, making our findings applicable to similar quantum-based sampling tasks such as the IQP computation model, which may be useful in short-term experiments and provide guidance for long-term studies attempting to demonstrate quantum superiority. Given the complexity and precision issues associated with calculating higher-order terms, developing various resummation methods has become crucial in minimizing computational costs while producing accurate thermodynamic estimates. A recent breakthrough presented a resummation method to all orders of the chemical potential by incorporating charge density correlation functions into the Taylor series. However, since these correlation functions are calculated stochastically from various random volume sources, biased estimates arise which significantly skew results, especially for large values of the number of correlation functions and the chemical potential. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Additionally, the article introduces a novel concept of Euclidean spaces with a function of betweenness and assigns them a unique topological structure, thus providing a potential candidate for the embedding space required by Menger's problem. Ultimately, the article demonstrates that this new Euclidean space with a function of betweenness is topologically equivalent to the familiar \(\mathfrak{Y}^2\) space and, upon embedding, retains the property of being compact. Further, the article proves that any space with the property of betweenness can be embedded into a Euclidean space with a function of betweenness, which is itself embeddable into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Finally, the article presents Menger's problem in its most general form and offers a solution valid for all metric spaces. This solution had previously been addressed by other researchers in specific contexts but was absent a unified solution until now.

To overcome this limitation, a new approach called reverse compression has been developed. Reverse compression method applies universally to both classical and quantum information processes, relying solely on the channel to be used. All input data leading to indistinguishable outputs are compressed to a single state, regardless of their prior distribution. Furthermore, reverse compression can be viewed as a higher order preprocessing operation. We examine its applicability to erasure channels, revealing that while noiseless reverse compression may only occur in trivial scenarios, meaningful instances of noisy reverse compression are indeed possible. We demonstrate that the amount of noisy reverse compression achievable is upper limited by the square root of the measure of discord, a key indicator of quantum entanglement. We further explore noisy reverse compression in the context of entangled qubit pairs, illustrating that the amount of noisy reverse compression can be substantial and relating it to established metrics of quantum correlation. We now demonstrate the possibility of actively generating reverse compression using quantum memory, termed active reverse compression, illustrating its occurrence in an entanglement-based swapping process. We conclude by discussing the potential link between active reverse compression and the unique characteristics of quantum erasure, including the ability to simultaneously delete and retain quantum information. We examine the possibility of active reverse compression in multiparticle systems, showcasing a process involving three qubits that achieves reverse compression. Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event frequencies, to provide
more precise predictions. Experimental findings, drawn from two real-world
processes, demonstrate that neural networks outperform a benchmark case and
reveal differences in performance across distinct process events and scenarios. 
Our investigation into the impact of process events on neural network performance
suggests that models perform better with more diverse event sets but may struggle
with isolated or frequent events. Overall, our study offers valuable
insights for applying deep learning to process prediction tasks. Our open-source
code and shared knowledge enable other researchers to replicate our results. Our
work also outlines future avenues for exploring deep learning in process mining. 
The code for the experiments is available at https://github.com/eugenioaraujo/prediction-process-mining.

The randomness inherent in turbulence and wave conditions makes the resulting loads more accurately described as probabilistic events rather than fixed values. The effect of these stochastic factors on the loads is also contingent on the prevailing environmental conditions, with variations occurring more noticeably under higher mean wind speeds than lower ones, a characteristic known as heteroscedasticity. The conventional deterministic and stochastic surrogates are ineffective in capturing this variability, leading to an inaccurate portrayal of the structure's response. By leveraging recent advancements in statistical inference, a novel heteroscedastic surrogate model can be trained from a database containing noise to forecast the conditional probability density function of the responses. The proposed model, which incorporates the statistical characteristics of the 10-minute load data of the IEA-10MW-RWT subject to wind and wave forces, as simulated in OpenFAST, outperforms standard Gaussian process regression in terms of approximating the variance of the responses. Additionally, the model demonstrates a 60 percent improvement in accuracy when forecasting the 99th percentile of the responses compared to conventional surrogates. The resulting model can be utilized to determine design loads, inform sampling strategies, and conduct reliability analyses. The implementation of this novel model is a crucial step towards enabling reliability-based design and other advanced structural analysis techniques for offshore wind turbines. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi identifier. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. The correct operator to use in parameterization is actually the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi identifier, and solving this problem requires a thorough grasp of Riemanian geometry and the integration of differential forms. This problem has a particularly striking outcome when considering elliptic operators, as they require an important simplification known as de Rham's theorem. As an application, this paper provides a comprehensive solution to a problem initially proposed by J.C. Maxwell in 1901, along with other results from the late 1800s

Existing methods for adjusting a robot's trajectory or impedance have focused on specific uncertainties, such as detecting human intentions or uncertainty-based learning from demonstration. These approaches fall short in addressing multiple uncertainties that commonly occur in tasks. This study introduces a more comprehensive framework to improve adaptability - using model predictive control (MPC) to simultaneously plan a robot's trajectory and impedance. These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems. The resulting class of methods, referred to as Continuous Runge-Kutta Methods (CRKMs), encompasses HBVMs as well as other energy-preserving methods such as continuous Galerkin methods. The connection between CRKMs and HBVMs is highlighted, and a broad class of CRKMs that does not necessarily maintain energy conservation is introduced. Technical aspects of implementing CRKMs, including choice of point estimators and building matrices, are examined in detail. The feasibility of extending CRKMs to semi-implicit time discretization is also investigated. The approach is illustrated by two examples: a semi-simple 2D Hamiltonian system and 3D Navier-Stokes equations. The efficiency of CRKMs is demonstrated through numerical experiments on these problems, showcasing its superiority to traditional methods in certain scenarios. The techniques explored here can be extended to other combinations of numerical methods, and new classes of energy-preserving methods, as evidenced by the general Hamiltonian BVM (2,2) method and others. efficiency, and scalability of modern computer systems is the high cost associated with moving data between the central processing unit and main memory.  A range of methods has been used to mitigate data movement costs, including the use of cache, scratchpad memory, and reconfigurable computing.  Although these techniques have been used to address the data movement issue for over a century, the subject remains largely presented in isolated forms, making it difficult for readers to gain a comprehensive understanding of the evolution and relationships between these methods, which we aim to rectify with this survey.  By examining historical context, we identify the key drivers behind data movement costs, and then examine how various computational paradigms have addressed this issue throughout their development.  We compare and contrast different computational paradigms and their associated mitigation techniques, and also discuss how they can be used in conjunction with other approaches, such as deep learning and model-driven design.  Based on a comprehensive analysis of 104 academic papers representing a century of research in this area, we hope that this survey provides a useful resource for researchers and developers seeking to mitigate data movement costs.  All associated data and code are publicly available, and we encourage researchers to build upon and extend this work, potentially by exploring new approaches for reconfigurable architectures, such as P4 programming, and related areas such as network functions, where data movement costs are particularly pronounced.  A public version of this survey, as well as an accompanying code base, are available at https://github

We introduce a concept of Schreier growth gap, a function that measures group growth, by examining its implications on G's set actions. We then explore Schreier growth gaps for solvable groups. If G is metabelian and finitely presented or torsion-free, but not virtually abelian, it possesses a Schreier growth gap of n^2. If metabelian G has a Krull dimension of k, it will have a Schreier growth gap of n^k, such as the Schreier growth gap n^d for the wreath product C_p ∋¬ ℤ^d and n^(d+1) for ℤ ∋¬ ℤ^d. considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. These assessments involve 10-stem multiple-choice questions that require the test-taker to anticipate the consequences of negation when presented with a mix of passage and question without the option to refer to the passage.

In the framework of classical systems, the Burgers vector serves as a measure of deformation within the medium, whereas at an atomic level, it is a fundamentally quantized property. A primary goal of this paper lies in exploring a novel approach for quantizing plane gravitational waves. However, the complex nature of these systems, particularly those studied in quantum chemistry and superconducting materials, means they are too difficult for classical computers to solve precisely either analytically or computationally. Since its inception in the 1980s, the primary goal of quantum computation has been the utilization of quantum computers to model such complex quantum systems. Furthermore, the possibility of obtaining valuable insights inaccessible through classical methods using fewer than a hundred qubits suggests that quantum simulation may be one of the earliest tangible applications of quantum computers. This document explores the theoretical and experimental progress in quantum simulation employing quantum computers from the inception of the concept to the ongoing intense research currently under way. We will examine the theoretical justification for the simulation of quantum systems utilizing quantum computers and review the latest advancements in both theoretical and experimental quantum simulation as well as the underlying quantum computing principles. We will also examine the challenges associated with quantum computation in the realm of quantum chemistry and chemically important processes, discussing the role of electronic structure and the incorporation of classical techniques, in addition to reviewing the current state of quantum simulation, particularly in the areas of fermionic systems, bosonic systems, and impurity systems, covering the key developments over the past decade. A notable benefit of GNNs is their ability to adapt to various challenges, which, although expanding their application range, also raises difficulties in selecting the most suitable model or acceleration technique for a given task. A particular challenge stems from the fact that the performance of a GNN model or acceleration technique generally hinges on the characteristics of the underlying graph. To address this issue of graph-dependent acceleration, this study proposes a data-driven model called ProGNNosis that can forecast the GNN training duration for a given model on an arbitrary graph by examining input graph metrics. ProGNNosis achieves this forecast by leveraging an offline-trained regression model based on a diverse synthetic graph dataset. By doing so, the approach enables users to make informed design decisions for a specific problem. A methodology to develop and apply ProGNNosis is described in the paper, which involves selecting a suitable graph representation for a given use case. Our findings indicate that ProGNNosis helps to achieve an average speedup of 1.22X compared to randomly selecting a graph representation in well-known GNN models, such as GCN, GIN, GAT, and GraphSAGE. Moreover, the analysis reveals that the value of new knowledge peaks earlier in sciences and later in humanities. To validate these findings, the research team used three alternative methods to analyze the literature evolution and found consistent results. These findings imply that the value of new knowledge gradually decreases as the literature grows, suggesting that the returns on new knowledge accumulate at a decreasing rate. This process involves pre-training a general model on a vast, unlabeled corpus, followed by fine-tuning on datasets of expert-labeled relevance information. The ideal IR system would integrate the perspectives of both users and the system to gauge relevance. The user-centric approach analyzes real users' behavior to determine relevance, whereas the system-centric approach relies on the expertise and signals provided by algorithms. Building on this user-system relevance dichotomy and the success of pre-trained models, this paper proposes Pre-Rank, a novel ranking framework that harmonizes the two perspectives within a pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm. However, their memory consumption has proven to be a major limitation, largely restricting their use to smaller-scale problems. In an effort to overcome this restriction, a novel variant of LSTM, called FlatLSTM, was developed, which eliminates the need for a balance between model performance and memory constraints by doing away with unnecessary layer complexity. As a result, a flat LSTM architecture is composed of a straightforward sequence of neurons with shared weights, similar to traditional feedforward networks. In this work, the method of optimizing flat LSTM weights was explored through the application of backpropagation with momentum, and the resulting models were compared to their traditional LSTM counterparts in several speech recognition tasks. The findings indicate that flat LSTM models are capable of producing nearly identical WERs to their traditional LSTM counterparts, but with a substantial reduction in memory consumption of up to 90%. Ontological frameworks, on the other hand, propose that the results of measurements remain unaffected by the procedures used to obtain them. However, quantum mechanics poses a significant challenge in this regard, due to its inherent ambiguity. Assuming that all measurement outcomes can be represented by the readings of pointers, any viable ontological model must unequivocally determine the positions of objects and pointers alike. Nevertheless, pointer positions become obscure in relativistic and cosmological contexts. Researchers have suggested alternative solutions to this issue, one of which involves using solutions derived from the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, specifically as proposed by Hartle and Hawking. We present such a model based on these solutions as its core ontology and demonstrate that any system incorporating these solutions as fundamental properties would render the global preservation of Lorentz invariance incompatible with the concept of global determinism. Nevertheless, we propose an Everett-inspired approach, where all possible mappings of matter fields onto geometric configurations and their diverse interpretations are equally real, offering a potential resolution to this paradox. Moreover, this model may hold implications for resolving the quantum gravity conundrums affecting black hole thought experiments, such as black holes in interaction with matter, ultimately providing insight into the relationship between determinism and the fundamental laws of physics. Lastly, we explore the implications of this model on the mind-body problem and suggest that an Everett-inspired interpretation may offer a more satisfactory answer to this question than other interpretations

We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. By combining the Celestial Mechanics Test for Small Bodies from the PLANCKO project with an extensive dataset of exoplanet characteristics, we reveal that smaller planets with masses between 1.7 and 10 Earth masses and orbital radii between 0.5 and 2.5 astronomical units are subjected to varying levels of celestial mechanic disturbances. Using a Gaussian Process emulator, we identify tidal dissipation as the predominant factor influencing these disturbances, followed by gravitational interactions with other stars in the system. Our analysis indicates that up to 30% of planets could experience some level of overlap with their host star's habitable zone due to dynamical effects, which could also promote or hinder atmospheric loss. We have also created a database showcasing various dynamical scenarios that could affect the habitability of planets, which could be accessed through the project website. The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.

The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.

The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile scene text models capable of providing more reliable and robust predictions.
